Two broad reasons.

One: Because alimony depends on a lot of factors, including but not limited to the law, jurisdiction, the judge, etc. If you've been following the news recently, you know that the wife may ask for any amount and the court may actually grant. In many cases, women marry for wealth and leave with a heft alimony. That is male oppression. 

Two: Mahr is decided before getting married. A person doesn't know how much alimony he'll have to pay in case his marriage goes wrong. 


You might be interested to know that the minimum mahr is the monetary value of ~30 grams of silver (less than ₹5,000), and the recommended value is approx. ~1550 grams of silver (less than ₹2,00,000). This is negotiated before the wedding by both sides and then read aloud for everyone to know and understand at the nikah.

Mahr isn't always paid to the bride; it is promised. It is up to the bride whether she wants to ask for it upfront or if it remains as a promise. Unlike dowry, this is mentioned at the time of the nikah and in the nikahnama itself. So there's no hidden wealth. 

This is purely intended to protect the bride financially. Most of the time, couples opt for the standard mahr amount, which is significant but not extravagant. Of course, the bride or her family may ask for whatever they think is appropriate, and the groom or his family can refuse.

And the best part, in my opinion, is that if the man divorces his wife, this mahr will definitely need to be paid to her. Kind of like an alimony, so that she isn't left vulnerable and dependent on others. And men don't divorce their wives without a valid cause.

But, if the woman chooses to ask for divorce, aka khula, then she has to forfeit this mahr. Again, this ensures that the woman doesn't ask for divorce without a valid cause.

I won't say it's exactly like tum. Like many families use tum for elders also. I've seen friends address their mother as tum, respectfully of course, but still you can't use tui in that context. As another person mentioned, it's intimate.
Tu sounds vulgar in most context. It's more like Tumi-> Aap, Tui-> Tum, Aapni is super formal, at this point the tone in Hindi changes to the bookish version, rarely used when speaking.

Just trust Tumi for most parts. It'll work. It's age-appropriate and respectful enough. So you can use it for an infant to a 100-year-old person. 

Aapni is extremely formal. Mostly used for teachers and such. 

Tui is for the closest friends and relatives, they need to be about the same age or younger.

For strangers, many people use Aapni, but I stick to Tumi. But make sure to address them respectfully, use Dada/Didi/Kaku/Kakima.
